name: bijogo, parler de Bijante, île de Bubaque = dialecte kagbaaga
confidence_why: The record rests on Segerer's 2000 thesis (published 2002), the only first-hand grammar of Bubaque Bijogo, whose accent chapter finds a pitch accent of unpredictable position and no lexical tone; Rose (2010) restates this, and the only divergent analysis, Wilson's unpublished two-tone outline cited by Pozdniakov and Segerer (2025), concerns the Kajooko lect of Uno and Orango rather than the Bubaque variety recorded here.

new_statements.quote: Le bijogo est une langue à accent. Il s'agit surtout d'un accent de hauteur mais aussi, dans une certaine mesure, d'intensité. Il est porté par la syllabe, qui peut être réduite à une consonne nasale. L'hypothèse tonale, bien que préférée par certains (notamment Wilson 2001), n'est pas retenue [...] La position de l'accent semble cependant arbitraire, même si sa présence est prévisible. Ses trop nombreuses variations nous ont incité à ne pas le noter dans la suite de la description, excepté dans les cas où il joue un rôle morphologique précis, comme dans certains domaines du système verbal. [p.29:] L'accent échappe pour l'instant à toute tentative de systématisation.
new_statements.translation: Bijogo is an accent language. It is mainly a pitch accent but also, to some extent, an intensity accent. It is carried by the syllable, which may be reduced to a nasal consonant. The tonal hypothesis, though preferred by some (notably Wilson 2001), is not adopted [...] The position of the accent nevertheless seems arbitrary, even if its presence is predictable. Its too numerous variations led us not to mark it in the rest of the description, except where it plays a precise morphological role, as in certain areas of the verbal system. [p.29:] The accent for now escapes any attempt at systematisation.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same analysis as the catalog record (Segerer 2000 thesis, coded 'variable'): pitch(-and-intensity) accent, position in nouns unpredictable, tonal reading rejected, morphological use in the verb system. The 2002 book is the published revision and adds: the explicit five-point argument against Wilson's (2001) H/L tone analysis, the 3% secondary-accent figure for short nouns, the accent~vowel-length 'affinité par exclusion' with the présence/position table (p.30), and main accent on verbal prefix bá- with an unstable secondary accent (p.228). Compatible with the Rose [2010] statement held by the project ('accent- or stress-, rather than tone-based'); it contradicts only Wilson…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bijogo (Bubaque/Bijante, kagbaaga) has a word accent realised mainly by pitch and partly by intensity; every noun carries one (presence predictable) but its position cannot be predicted and fluctuates between citation and context forms; no accentual minimal pairs among lexemes; a two-tone analysis (Wilson 2001) is explicitly rejected. In the verbal system accent placement is morphological/distinctive: má-da 'you came' vs ma-dá 'come!', ú-da 'he comes' vs u-dá 'it is he who comes'; in complex forms the main accent sits on the prefix bá-. Accent and vowel length are near-complementary (accent: presence predictable, position arbitrary; length: presence arbitrary, position mostly penultimate) and jointly serve a demarcative function.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.28: citation forms of short nouns (up to 3 syllables, 82% of nouns) only exceptionally (3%) show more than one accented syllable; in that case a primary and a secondary accent can be recognised. p.228: in complex verb forms a secondary accent (noted with a macron) can oppose ya-bá-da¯ 'they will come' (inaccompli) to ya¯-bá-da 'if they come' (accompli); 'L'accent secondaire est instable et n'a été observé qu'avec les indices de classe comportant la voyelle a.'
new_statements.exceptions: p.29: accent tends to fall on a short vowel / an accented vowel tends not to be long, with exceptions Æ-táákø 'lune, mois', ka-™áákÆ 'chasse', ka-gbóóna 'champ'; accent and lengthening can both be used expressively (dikidik 'tous' realised [díkídík], [dikíídik] or [díkíídík]); p.228: accent does not disambiguate most simple verb forms (yá-da 'ils viennent' ~ 'ils sont venus').
new_statements.identity_note: The book describes the kagbaaga (central) dialect of Bijogo as spoken in the village of Bijante on Bubaque island (printed p.13: 'Centre : kagbaaga, dialecte de Bubaque, Rubane et Soga'; 'la présente description se limite au parler du village de Bijante') = bidy1244 exactly. Other dialects (kajoko Orango/Uno, kamøna Caravela, kañaki Canhabaque) appear only in the consonant-correspondence overview p.30; no prosody is given for them.

audit.reasoning: The record's deciding quotation is confirmed verbatim, at the stated pages, in the open-access thesis PDF we hold (via the glyph-decoded chapter 6). The source is the only modern first-hand description of Bijogo, a 452-pp reference grammar (thesis form) with an explicit, quantified accent section; Glottolog's top-ranked grammar entries are this same work and its 2002 Peeters revision. Web search (HAL, Oxford Guide 2025 TOC, MUN Niger-Congo verbal-categories chapter) turned up no independent prosodic or instrumental study; the one secondary source downloaded restates Segerer ('accent- or stress-, rather than tone-based'). The 'variable' coding (free/unpredictable pitch accent position, statistical final/penult tendencies, no phonological status) faithfully reflects Segerer's analysis, including his own caveat that a tonal analysis cannot be fully excluded.
